claims.claim: Accepted name Dracaena trifasciata; Sansevieria trifasciata is a synonym.

g.note: 12 Nov: POWO blocked automated access (403). GBIF backbone: 'Sansevieria trifasciata Prain' status SYNONYM, accepted species Dracaena trifasciata. Wikidata Q65936984 gives POWO id urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:77164235-1. NC State: former name Sansevieria trifasciata.

claims.claim: Arabic names لسان الحماة and نبتة الثعبان are used for this plant.

g.note: 12 Nov: Wikidata Arabic label is the botanical 'ذلب ثلاثي الأحزمة'; no source for the two common names on the page.

u.note: Owner: confirm what UAE customers call it in Arabic (لسان الحماة, نبتة الثعبان or others).

claims.claim: Best in bright indirect light, such as near an east-facing window (Clemson: bright indirect light in the mornings); survives low light but grows slowly and colour fades; suits bedrooms, living-room corners, offices and reception areas.

g.note: PSU: 'enjoys bright indirect light but tolerates low-light areas very well'. CSU: 'medium to bright indirect light but will adapt to low light'; variegation less pronounced in low light. UA: survives very low light but may not grow. 12 Nov (SEO follow-up): Clemson HGIC (opened): snake plant 'ideal lighting ... bright, indirect'; window breakdown: east-facing 'Bright indirect light in the mornings', north-facing 'Lowest levels of light. No direct sun is present all day'. No snake plant source names a north window or a bathroom.

u.note: Baseline sun-through-glass: tinted tower glazing lowers indoor light, so 'bright indirect' near a window is right.

claims.change: 12 Nov: 'east- or north-facing window' changed to 'east-facing window', named to Clemson Extension (north = lowest light, not bright indirect). 'A bathroom with a window works well too' removed: no source opened (NC State, PSU, CSU, Illinois, UConn, Clemson, UGA) mentions bathrooms.

claims.claim: Bright indirect light; gentle morning sun is fine; avoid harsh midday/afternoon summer sun through west- or south-facing glass; filter it with a sheer curtain or move the plant back from the glass.

g.note: NC State: direct sun 'only part of the day, 2 to 6 hours' (so gentle sun is fine). PSU: keep out of direct sun, 'it can burn'. 12 Nov (SEO follow-up): Clemson: 'Avoid direct and hot sunlight on the plant as this can lead to burning of the leaves'. UGA B1318: southern exposure gives the largest variation of light and heat; 'Southern and western exposures are interchangeable'. Wisconsin Extension (general houseplant light advice): medium bright light 'such as in an east facing window', or a sheer curtain or distance from the glass in south and west windows. No source says a curtain alone is 'enough', so the page no longer says it.

u.note: Baseline summer-heat, sun-through-glass. Local nurseries recommend shade cloth outdoors.

claims.change: Light fact allows gentle morning sun (NC State: some direct sun is tolerated). 12 Nov: sunburn signs no longer give 'within a few days' (our estimate). 12 Nov (SEO follow-up): 'A sheer curtain on the window is enough to stop the sunburn' (overstated) changed to 'Filter that sun with a sheer curtain, or move the plant back from the glass' (Wisconsin Extension).

claims.where: quick_answer, quick_facts.Water, care_sections.watering, uae_year, mistakes, myths, first_week, faqs.outdoors
claims.claim: Water only when the soil is dry to the bottom of the pot; test with a skewer before each watering; small/terracotta pots in warm bright spots dry faster, large plastic pots in dim AC rooms slower, coastal humidity slower, inland heat faster; less in the cool months (NC State: every one to two months in winter; Illinois: just enough to stop the leaves shrivelling). Overwatering and root rot are the main reason it fails.

g.note: PSU: 'Water only when it is dry'; 'You can kill it by overwatering'; root rot 'a common affliction'. NC State: 'In winter only water every one to two months'. Illinois: 'allow the soil to dry completely between watering'; winter 'just enough to keep the foliage from shriveling'; 'Over-watering is the main reason for failure'. CSU is softer in winter (keep the soil from drying out completely); the skewer test covers both. Month labels: sources give no months, only 'winter' (NC State, Illinois) and 'fall and winter when active growth slows' (CSU). The page uses one UAE split for watering and feeding: growth Mar–Oct, slower Nov–Feb (see c08).

u.note: No UAE interval is stated any more. The rule and test work in any home; drying factors match baseline indoor-ac (not reliably dry) and summer-heat.

claims.change: 12 Nov: removed our intervals (every 2–3 weeks Apr–Oct, 4–6 weeks Nov–Mar) from the quick answer, quick facts, watering section, summer and winter cards, mistakes and myths, and 'wait another week'. Now rule + skewer test + what changes it, with the NC State winter figure named. 'Most often dies from overwatering' now 'main reason it fails' (Illinois). 12 Nov (SEO follow-up): quick-facts labels 'Apr–Oct' / 'Nov–Mar' changed to 'Mar–Oct' / 'Nov–Feb' to match the feeding months; autumn card now says growth slows from November.

claims.claim: UAE tap water is desalinated and remineralised; mineral content varies. A white crust or brown tips mean salts: flush the pot with plenty of water, or use filtered water.

g.note: CSU 1339: brown leaf tips and a whitish crust on the pot or soil are signs of salts from water and fertiliser; flush by filling the pot with water a couple of times.

u.note: Baseline tap-water (low confidence; hardness disputed). The page does not call the water hard.

claims.change: Was 'UAE tap water is hard'. Now desalinated and remineralised, mineral content varies; flushing tied to symptoms. 12 Nov: ledger note corrected (no 'often hard' on the page).

claims.claim: Fast-draining cactus/succulent mix or potting soil with plenty of perlite or coarse sand; pot with a drainage hole; terracotta and cement dry faster than plastic.

g.note: PSU: 'cactus potting mix or one with perlite'; 'only containers with drainage holes'. CSU: often grown in clay pots for stability.

u.note: Linked products exist in the store.

claims.change: 12 Nov: 'half and half with perlite' (no source for the ratio) changed to 'plenty of perlite or coarse sand'.

claims.claim: Half-strength all-purpose fertiliser once a month in the growing season (Mar–Oct in the UAE); none Nov–Feb; too much fertiliser causes brown tips and salt build-up.

g.note: PSU: 'fertilize monthly during the growing season with an all-purpose fertilizer at half strength'. CSU 1339: over-applied salt-based fertiliser causes brown tips. Months: PSU says only 'growing season'; NC State 'spring to autumn' vs 'winter'; CSU growth slows in 'fall and winter'. The page maps this to one UAE split, used for both watering and feeding: growth Mar–Oct, slower Nov–Feb (quick facts, fertiliser section, autumn/winter/spring cards, problems, mistakes).

u.note: Baseline seasons: growth season to Oct–Apr outdoors; indoor AC plants grow through summer, so Mar–Oct fits. Nov–Feb is the coolest part of the year on the coast (baseline coastal-winter: January lows about 14–16 °C; inland-winter colder). It is a calendar mapping of 'winter', not a plant interval.

claims.change: 12 Nov: the monthly figure now names Penn State Extension in the fertiliser section. 12 Nov (SEO follow-up): mistakes[6] 'balanced fertiliser' changed to 'all-purpose fertiliser' (Penn State wording); watering labels aligned to the same Mar–Oct / Nov–Feb split.

claims.where: care_sections.repotting (paragraphs and steps), uae_year.Autumn, mistakes, myths
claims.claim: Repot only when roots fill the pot (PSU: about every 5 years, 'Hahnii' every 3); go up one pot size (CSU: 1–2 in, about 2.5–5 cm wider); a much larger pot holds wet soil; best Oct–Nov or Feb–Apr, not the summer peak; let a new plant settle first; do not water straight away after cutting roots.

g.note: PSU: repot 'every 5 years or so'; 'Hahnii' 'every 3 years'. CSU 1316: pot 'only one to two inches larger in diameter'; roots growing out of the bottom mean repot. VT: succulent cuttings 'will rot if kept too moist' (basis for letting cut roots seal). CSU 1316 says to soak general houseplants after repotting, so the page ties the wait only to cut roots, with no number.

u.note: Baseline seasons: repotting in the cooler months.

claims.change: v1 'every 2–3 years' changed to the PSU figures. 12 Nov: '3–5 cm wider' (our figure) changed to CSU 1–2 in (2.5–5 cm), named; 'wait about a week before watering' and 'first few weeks after arrival' (our wait times) changed to rules.

claims.claim: Division is easiest and keeps a yellow edge; leaf cuttings: 5–8 cm sections, slanted lower cut, let the cut ends dry, upright in barely damp soil (rot if too wet) or in water; about three months to root and shoot (University of Arkansas, named); yellow-edged cuttings grow back green.

g.note: PSU: 'most easily propagated by division'. VT: '2-inch sections', 'lower cut slanted', variegated shoots lose variegation, rot if too moist. UA: 'three-inch long segments'; 'In about three months, the plants will root and send up a new shoot'. UF/IFAS (archived): 'Laurentii' must be propagated by division to keep variegation (periclinal chimeras). UConn: cuttings root in water.

claims.change: v2.0 had 8–10 cm, dry 2–3 days, 4–8 weeks. Now 5–8 cm (VT, UA). 12 Nov: 'dry a day or two' and 'wait about a week' (our wait times; no primary source opened) changed to 'until the cut ends form a dry skin'; three months now names UA Extension.

claims.claim: Grows well at normal room temperature; copes with summer heat in shade if the soil dries; protect from cold below about 10–13 °C, especially inland and in colder GCC cities.

g.note: NC State: tolerates 'cool temperatures around 50 degrees' (10 °C). UConn: 'avoid anything below 55 degrees F' (13 °C). UF/IFAS: chilling damage, keep at 45 °F or above. Illinois: 'moderate to warm temperatures'. 15–24 °C (said to be RHS) could not be found: RHS page 404. 12 Nov (SEO follow-up) re-opened: NC State 'tolerates ... cool temperatures around 50 degrees'; UConn 'avoid anything below 55 degrees F'. The range 10–13 °C covers both.

u.note: Baseline inland-winter and gcc-winter; summer-heat for outdoor shade. Winter card and outdoors FAQ: inland lows of 3–5 °C and Riyadh/Kuwait lows of 7–10 °C fall below this range; coastal lows (14–16 °C) do not.

claims.change: Inland/GCC cold warning added (v2). 12 Nov: 'Prefers 15–24 °C' removed (source not found); 'below 10 °C' widened to 'about 10–13 °C' (NC State, UConn). 12 Nov (SEO follow-up): uae_year Winter and faqs.outdoors 'below 10 °C' changed to 'below about 10–13 °C' to match quick facts and the sources.

claims.claim: Tolerates low humidity; in humid coastal homes the soil dries more slowly, so water less often.

g.note: NC State: 'tolerates low humidity'. Illinois: 'low humidity'.

u.note: Baseline indoor-ac: UAE AC rooms are not reliably dry (Sharjah study 60.7% RH).

claims.change: Removed 'dry AC air' and 'any humidity'. 12 Nov: 'Prefers lower humidity' changed to 'Tolerates low humidity' (NC State wording).

claims.claim: Keep the plant out of the direct stream of cold air from an AC vent; test: with the AC on, hold a hand next to the leaves; if the air moves, move the plant or turn the louvres.

g.note: UF/IFAS (archived): cold injury; 'Prevent plant exposure to cold air or cold water'. No source gives a safe distance, so none is given. Cold draughts as a cause of brown tips is not in any primary source and was removed from the brown tips card.

u.note: Baseline ac-vents is low confidence (nursery experience). Owner: confirm that AC draughts damage snake plants in customers' homes and that the hand test is good advice.

claims.change: 12 Nov: '1 m from a direct vent' (our estimate) removed from quick facts and mistakes; replaced by the rule and a hand test. AC draught removed as a brown-tip cause and fix.

claims.claim: Outdoors in full shade May–Sep; test the soil more often in heatwaves (small and terracotta pots dry fastest); move between AC and outdoors gradually, short spells in full shade first, slower in the hottest months and from a dim room; pale patches mean go back into shade. Grows well outdoors October to April.

g.note: PSU: direct sun 'can burn'. NC State: some direct sun tolerated. Gradual acclimatisation is standard practice to prevent sunscorch; no source gives a time, so none is given.

u.note: Baseline summer-heat and seasons. Owner: confirm from PlantsWorld experience that shaded outdoor snake plants survive UAE summers and that customers grow them outdoors Oct–Apr.

claims.change: 12 Nov: 'check every few days in heatwaves' and 'over a week or two, a few hours in shade' (our estimates) removed; now rule + what to watch + what changes it.

claims.claim: Toxic to cats and dogs (ASPCA); saponins; nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea; keep away from pets and young children; call a vet or 24-hour clinic straight away if chewed.

g.note: ASPCA (opened 12 Nov): 'Toxic to Dogs, Toxic to Cats'; toxic principle 'Saponins'; signs 'Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea'. NC State lists children as affected.

claims.change: Removed 'drooling', which ASPCA does not list; signs now match ASPCA. Added young children and 'call your vet if your pet eats any'; removed 'usually mild'.

claims.claim: Takes in carbon dioxide at night (CAM); one plant will not noticeably change the air in a room.

g.note: Karunananda & Abeysinghe 2019 (SLJFA): S. trifasciata showed net CO2 decrease in darkness; stomata open at night (CAM). Drexel/Cummings: plants do not measurably change room air.

claims.claim: Older plants occasionally flower: small, fragrant, greenish-white to cream flowers; indoor plants rarely flower.

g.note: NC State: flowers 'greenish-white to cream-colored, sticky, and fragrant'; 'rarely blooms' as a houseplant. UA: 'Old plants occasionally flower'. 'Open in the evening' only on Wikipedia (fragrant at night); 'sign of a root-bound plant' had no source.

claims.change: 12 Nov: removed 'open in the evening' and 'a sign of a healthy, slightly root-bound plant'; added 'indoor plants rarely flower' (NC State).

claims.claim: Can be kept in water (roots only) and leaf cuttings root in water; change the water often (UConn: daily for rooting cuttings); grows slower and less reliably than in soil.

g.note: UConn: 'place the cuttings in water to take root (change the water daily for best results)'. UF/IFAS Santa Rosa (search result): best grown in a soil-based potting mix. Long-term water culture is anecdotal, so the page says 'less reliably'.

u.note: PlantsWorld sells it as a water plant.

claims.change: Softened long-term water culture claim. 12 Nov: 'change the water every week' (our interval) replaced by 'often', with the UConn figure named.

claims.claim: Lives for many years; about 15 cm ('Hahnii') to 120 cm (tall types) indoors; slow growth indoors, slower in low light.

g.note: PSU: species 'up to 4 feet tall', 'Hahnii' 'only 6 inches'. UA: 'slow growth'. NC State lists growth rate as medium (outdoor attribute), so the page says 'slow indoors'. Many years: PSU repot interval of 5 years implies a long-lived pot plant.

claims.change: '10+ years' removed. 12 Nov: size '30–120 cm' corrected to 15–120 cm (PSU); growth 'Slow' to 'Slow indoors, slower in low light'.

claims.claim: Problem causes and fixes: root rot from overwatering (remove soil, cut black roots, let cut ends dry, repot dry, water only when the soil tests dry); brown tips from salts in tap water or fertiliser (flush, filtered water, less fertiliser, trim tips that do not regrow); wrinkling from thirst or root damage (water; if leaves do not firm up, check roots); flopping from overwatering, low light or a light pot (heavier pot); sunburn patches do not heal; slow growth is normal in low light and winter.

g.note: PSU: root rot from overwatering; heavy pot for tall plants. Illinois: winter water just enough to stop shrivelling (thirst causes wrinkling). CSU 1339: brown tips and crust from salts; flush. CSU: plants get top heavy, grown in clay pots for stability.

u.note: Owner: confirm these are the problems UAE customers report (WhatsApp chats) and add any missing ones.

claims.change: 12 Nov: removed our timings ('dry 1–2 days', 'wait one week', 'firm up within a week', 'within a few days of a move', 'new shoots in spring and autumn'); 'hard tap water' changed to 'minerals in tap water'; uneven watering and AC draughts removed as brown-tip causes (no primary source).

claims.claim: A snake plant is a common housewarming, Eid and corporate gift in the UAE because it forgives missed waterings and suits modern homes and offices.

g.note: PSU: forgiving, low-maintenance; tolerates going a month without water. Feng shui claim: only lifestyle sources, and they disagree (some call it bad feng shui), so removed.

u.note: Owner: confirm from PlantsWorld sales that customers buy it for housewarming, Eid and corporate gifts.

claims.change: 12 Nov: removed 'in feng shui it is seen as protective and bringing good energy' (no reliable source; sources disagree).

claims.claim: In a windowless room it survives only under bright electric light that is on for long hours, growing very slowly; in a dark room it uses up its reserves and dies.

g.note: UConn: plants 'do need some light to photosynthesize'; in dark corners they 'hang on for a few months, but then eventually run out of stored resources and die'. UNL Extension: 12 to 16 hours of supplemental light daily. UA: survives very low light but may not grow.

u.note: Fits UAE offices and flats with interior rooms lit most of the day.

claims.change: 12 Nov: 'give it a few weeks near a window from time to time' (our interval) replaced by 'move it to a window if it stops growing, fades or leans'.

claims.claim: A snake plant does not noticeably clean the air of a normal room; the sealed-chamber results do not scale to homes.

g.note: 12 Nov re-check (abstract opened, Europe PMC, PMID 31695112): 12 chamber studies, 196 results; median single-plant CADR 0.023 m3/h, 'necessitating the placement of 10-1000 plants/m2 of a building's floor space' to match outdoor-to-indoor air exchange in typical buildings (~1 h-1). Primary-source figure: 10-1,000 plants per m2. The Drexel news release (opened 12 Nov) says 'between 100 and 1,000 plants per square meter'; that is the press office's rounding, not the paper. Use the paper's figure if a number is shown. The guide gives no number. Earlier note said 100-1,000 (Drexel) and called 10-1,000 wrong; that correction was itself wrong and is reverted. Drexel also: 'reviewed a dozen studies, spanning 30 years'.

u.note: Not climate-dependent.

claims.claim: Snake plants do not need misting; water left in the leaf centre can rot the base; wipe dust off with a damp cloth.

g.note: CSU: 'Care should be taken to not pour water into the center of the rosette.' UConn: 'dust them manually'. No source recommends misting.

u.note: Humid coastal homes make standing water in the rosette slower to dry, so the advice holds more strongly.

claims.claim: Laurentii has yellow edges; Zeylanica is dark green with grey-green bands and no yellow edge; Hahnii is a compact rosette; starfish (S. cylindrica 'Starfish') has thick round leaves fanning out; all need the same care. 'Hahnii' needs repotting more often than tall types (Penn State: every 3 years).

g.note: UF/IFAS (archived; live URL now 404): 'Laurentii' 'showy golden yellow leaf margin'; 'Hahnii' birdnest rosette; 'Most plants sold as Sansevieria zeylanica are S. trifasciata'. PSU: 'Hahnii' repot every 3 years; Dracaena angolensis (cylindrica).

claims.claim: On arrival: bright indirect light away from direct sun and AC vents; leave it in one spot; test the soil before the first watering; do not repot straight away, only when roots fill the pot.

g.note: Restates c03, c05, c09 and c13. 'Moving it again and again slows the settling in' is general practice; low risk.

u.note: Same checks as c05 and c13. Store facts (damage reports) are in the KB (KB016), not on the page.

claims.change: 12 Nov: 'often does not need water for the first week or two', 'do not repot for a few weeks' and 'needs a few days' (our wait times) replaced by the soil test and rules. Ledger claim no longer mentions the WhatsApp/24 h store fact, which is not on the page.

claims.claim: ZZ plant: bright indirect light, copes with low light, water when soil fully dry, toxic (calcium oxalate). Golden pothos: bright indirect, survives low light, let soil dry between waterings, toxic. Peace lily: partial to deep shade, no direct sun, moist not soggy, toxic. Areca palm: bright indirect light, moist not soggy in the growing season, non-toxic to cats and dogs (ASPCA).

g.note: Opened 12 Nov. NC State: ZZ bright indirect, tolerates very low light, soil dry between waterings, calcium oxalate. Pothos: bright indirect, survives low light, dry between watering. Peace lily: 'partial to deep shade', 'moist, but not soggy'. Areca: bright indirect, moist not soggy in the growing season. ASPCA: pothos and peace lily toxic (calcium oxalates); areca non-toxic to cats, dogs and horses. NC State tags areca non-toxic too but warns about the terminal bud; the page says 'Non-toxic (ASPCA)'.

u.note: Indoor light and watering rules apply under UAE AC, as for the snake plant (baseline indoor-ac, sun-through-glass).

claims.claim: Fit lists: forgiving of missed waterings, copes with low light and AC rooms, slow growth; toxic if chewed; needs drainage and infrequent watering; rarely flowers.

g.note: Each item restates c03, c05, c15, c17 and c19. PSU: tolerates going 'a month or so' without water. Illinois: over-watering is the main reason for failure.

u.note: Same UAE checks as c05 and c13.

claims.claim: White cotton at the leaf base is mealybugs (sap-sucking); isolate the plant, dab with an alcohol-soaked cotton bud, spray with a houseplant product such as neem as the label directs. Tiny flies are fungus gnats from wet soil: let the soil dry, use yellow sticky traps.

g.note: CSU: mealybugs 'suck sap'; 'Swabbing individual mealybugs with alcohol'; quarantine new plants; neem 'may suppress'; fungus gnats favoured by 'excessively moist soil', let the surface dry, 'captured on sticky cards'. ISU: 'dab each one with an alcohol-soaked cotton swab'; sprays incl. neem; 'follow label directions'. NC State: monitor for mealybugs. Sand top layer: no source opened gives it, removed.

u.note: Not climate-dependent; neem product sold in the store.

claims.change: 12 Nov: split from c20. 'Neem once a week for 3–4 weeks' (our interval) replaced by 'as the label directs, until no new mealybugs appear'; 1–2 cm sand or pebble layer removed (no primary source).
